<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader||VARIATIONS, CALCULUS OF|917}}</noinclude>[[File:eb1911 v27 p0943 c1f1.png|center|139px]]


ds an important result, which may be stated ationary curves of the integral be drawn from the same initial point <math>\text{A}</math> to points <math>\text{P}</math>, <math>\text{Q}</math>, which are near together, and let the line <math>\text{PQ}</math> be of length <math>\nu</math>, and make an angle <math>\omega</math> with the axis of <math>x</math> (fig. 1). The excess of the integral taken along <math>\text{AQ}</math>, from <math>\text{A}</math> to <math>\text{Q}</math>, above the integral taken along <math>\text{AP}</math>, from <math>\text{A}</math> to <math>\text{P}</math>, is expressed, correctly to the first order in <math>\nu</math>, by the formula
{{block center|<math>\nu \cos \omega \left\{ \text{F}(x,\ y,\ y') + (\tan \omega - y')\frac{\partial \text{F}}{\partial y'} \right\}</math>.}}
In this formula <math>x</math>, <math>y</math> are the co-ordinates of <math>\text{P}</math>, and <math>y'</math> has the value belonging to the point <math>\text{P}</math> and the stationary curve <math>\text{AP}</math>. When the coefficient of <math>\nu \cos \omega</math> in the formula vanishes, the curve AP is said to be cut ''transversely'' by the line PQ, and a curve which cuts a family of stationary curves transversely is described as a {{smaller|'''''Transversals of stationary curves.'''''}} ''transversal'' of those curves. In the problem of variable limits, when a terminal point moves on a given guiding curve, the integral cannot be an extremum unless the stationary curve along which it is taken is cut transversely by the guiding curve at the terminal point. A simple example is afforded by the shortest line, drawn on a surface, from a point to a given curve, lying on the surface. The required curve must be a geodesic, and it must cut the given curve at right angles.

The problem of variable limits may always be treated by a method of which the following is the principle: In the First Problem let the initial point <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> be fixed, and let the terminal point {{smaller|'''''Alternative method.'''''}} <math>(x_1, y_1)</math> move on a fixed guiding curve <math>\text{C}_1</math>. Now, whatever the terminal point may be, the integral cannot be an extremum unless it is taken along a stationary curve. We have then to choose among those stationary curves which are drawn from <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> to points of <math>\text{C}_1</math> that one which makes the integral an extremum. This can be done by expressing the value of the integral taken along a stationary curve from the point <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> to the point <math>(x_1, y_1)</math> in terms of the co-ordinates <math>x_1</math>, <math>y_1</math>, and then making this expression an extremum, in regard to variations of <math>x_1</math>, <math>y_1</math>, by the methods of the differential calculus, subjecting <math>(x_1, y_1)</math> to the condition of moving on the curve <math>\text{C}_1</math>.

An important example of the first variation of integrals is afforded by the Principle of Least Action in dynamics. The kinetic energy <math>\text{T}</math> is a homogeneous function of the second degree in the differential coefficients <math>\dot{q}_1, \dot{q}_2, \dots \dot{q}_n</math> of the co-ordinates <math>q_1, q_2, \dots q_n</math> with respect to the time <math>t</math>, and the potential energy <math>\text{V}</math> is a function of these co-ordinates. The energy equation is of the form '''''Principle of least action.'''''

{{block center|<math>\text{T}+\text{V}=\text{E},</math>}}
where E is a constant. A ''course'' of the system is defined when the co-ordinates <math>q</math> are expressed as functions of a single parameter <math>\theta</math>. The ''action'' A of the system is defined as the integral <math>\int_{t_0}^{t_1}2\text{T}dt</math>, ''taken along a course'' from the initial position <math>(q^{(0)})</math> to the final position <math>(q^{(1)})</math>, but <math>t_0</math> and <math>t_1</math> are not fixed. The equations of motion are the principal equations answering to this integral. To obtain them it is most convenient to write <math>\Phi(\dot{q})</math> for T, and to express the integral in the form
{{block center|<math>\int_{\theta_0}^{\theta_1}2(\text{E}-\text{V})^{\frac{1}{2}}\{\Phi(q')\}^{\frac{1}{2}}d\theta,</math>}}
where <math>q'</math> denotes the differential coefficient of a co-ordinate <math>q</math> with respect to <math>\theta</math>, and, in accordance with the parametric method, the limits of integration are fixed, and the integrand is a homogeneous function of the <math>q'</math>'s of the first degree. There is then no difficulty in deducing the Lagrangian equations of motion of the type
{{block center|<math>\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial\text{T}}{\partial\dot{q}}-\frac{\partial\text{T}}{\partial q}+\frac{\partial\text{V}}{\partial q}=0.</math>}}
These equations determine the actual course of the system. Now if the system, in its actual course, passes from a given initial position <math>(q^{(0)})</math> to a variable final position <math>(q)</math>, the action A becomes a function of the <math>q</math>'s, and the first method used in the problem of variable limits shows that, for every <math>q</math>
{{block center|<math>\frac{\partial\text{A}}{\partial q}=\frac{\partial\text{T}}{\partial\dot{q}}.</math>}}
When the kinetic energy T is expressed as a homogeneous quadratic function of the momenta <math>\partial\text{T}/\partial\dot{q}</math>, say
{{block center|<math>\text{T}=\tfrac{1}{2}\Sigma_{r,\,s}\left(b_{rs}\frac{\partial\text{T}}{\partial\dot{q}_r}\frac{\partial\text{T}}{\partial\dot{q}_s}\right),\ (b_{sr}=b_{rs}),</math>}} and the differential coefficients of A are introduced instead of those of T, the energy equation becomes a non-linear partial differential equation of the first order for the determination of A as a function of the <math>q</math>’s. This equation is

{{block center|<math>\tfrac{1}{2}\Sigma_{r,\,s}\left(b_{rs}\frac{\partial \text{A}}{\partial q_r}\,\frac{\partial \text{A}}{\partial q_s}\right) + \text{V} = \text{E}.</math>}}

'''''Principle of varying action.'''''

A complete integral of this equation would yield an expression for A as a function of the <math>q</math>’s containing <math>n</math> arbitrary constants, <math>a_1, a_2, \dots a_n</math>, of which one <math>a_n</math> is merely additive to A; and the courses of the system which are compatible with the equations of motion are determined by equations of the form

{{block center|<math>\frac{\partial\text{A}}{\partial a_1} = b_1,\ \frac{\partial\text{A}}{\partial a_2} = b_2, \dots \frac{\partial\text{A}}{\partial a_{n-1}} = b_{n-1}</math>}}

where the <math>b</math>'s are new arbitrary constants. It is noteworthy that the differential equations of the second order by which the geodesics on an ellipsoid are determined were first solved by this method (C. G. J. Jacobi, 1839).

'''''Principle of varying action generalized.'''''

It has been proved that every problem of the calculus of variations, in which the integral to be made an extremum contains only one independent variable, admits of a similar transformation; that is to say, the integrals of the principal equations can always be obtained, in the way described above, from a complete integral of a partial differential equation of the first order, and this partial differential equation can always be formed by a process of elimination. These results were first proved by A. Clebsch (1858).

'''''Condition of integrability.'''''

Among other analytical developments of the theory of the first variation we may note that the necessary and sufficient condition that an expression of the form

{{block center|<math>\text{F}(x,\ y,\ y', \dots y^{(n)})</math>}}

should be the differential coefficient of another expression of the form

{{block center|<math>\text{F}_1(x,\ y,\ y', \dots y^{(n-1)})</math>}}

is the identical vanishing of the expression

{{block center|<math>\frac{\partial\text{F}}{\partial y} - \frac{d}{dx}\frac{\partial\text{F}}{\partial y'} + \frac{d^2}{dx^2}\frac{\partial\text{F}}{\partial y''} - \dots + (-1)^n \frac{d^n}{dx^n}\frac{\partial\text{F}}{\partial y^{(n)}}</math>.}} The result was first found by Euler (1744).

''Condition that a differential equation may arise from a problem of the calculus of variations.'' A differential equation

{{block center|<math>\phi(x, y, y', y'') = 0</math>}}

is the principal equation answering to an integral of the form

{{block center|<math>\int \text{F}(x, y, y')dx</math>}}

if the equation

{{block center|<math>\frac{d}{dx}\,\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y''} = \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y'}</math>}}

is satisfied identically. In the more general case of an equation of the form

{{block center|<math>\phi(x, y, y', \dots y^{(2n)}) = 0</math>}}

the corresponding condition is that the differential expression obtained by Lagrange's process of variation, viz.,

{{block center|<math>\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y}\,\delta y + \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y'}\,\frac{d\delta y}{dx} + \dots + \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y^{(2n)}}\,\frac{d^{2n}\delta y}{dx^{2n}},</math>}}

must be identical with the "adjoint" differential expression

{{block center|<math>\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y}\,\delta y - \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y'}\,\delta y\right) + \frac{d^2}{dx^2}\left(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y''}\,\delta y\right) - \dots + \frac{d^{2n}}{dx^{2n}}\left(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y^{(2n)}}\delta y\right).</math>}}

This matter has been very fully investigated by A. Hirsch (1897).

''First variation of a double integral.'' To illustrate the transformation of the first variation of multiple integrals we consider a double integral of the form

{{block center|<math>\int\int\psi(x, y, z, p, q, r, s, t)dxdy,</math>}}

taken over that area of the <math>z</math> plane which is bounded by a closed curve <math>s'</math>. Here <math>p</math>, <math>q</math>, . . . <math>t</math> denote the partial differential coefficients of <math>z</math> with respect to <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> of the first and second orders, according to the usual notation. When <math>z</math> is changed into <math>z + \epsilon w</math>, the terms of the first order in <math>\epsilon</math> are {{block center|<math>\epsilon\iint\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial z}w+\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial p}\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial q}\frac{\partial w}{\partial y}+\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial x^2}+\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial s}\frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial x\partial y}+\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}\frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial y^2}\right)dxdy.</math>}}
Each term must be transformed so that no differential coefficients of <math>w</math> are left under the sign of double integration. We exemplify the process by taking the term containing <math>\partial^2 w/\partial x^2</math>. We have
{{block center|<math>\iint\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial x^2}dxdy=\iint\left\{\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\right)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\right)\cdot\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\right\}dxdy</math>}}
{{block center|<math>=\iint\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\right)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left\{w\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\right)\right\}+w\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\right)\right]dxdy.</math>}}
The first two terms are transformed into a line integral taken round the boundary <math>s'</math>, and we thus find
{{block center|<math>\iint\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\frac{\partial^2 w}{\partial x^2}dxdy=\int\cos(x,\nu)\left\{\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}-w\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\right)\right\}ds'+\iint w\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\right)dxdy,</math>}}
where <math>\nu</math> denotes the direction of the normal to the edge <math>s'</math> drawn outwards. The double integral on the right-hand side contributes a term to the principal equation, and the line integral contributes terms to the boundary conditions. The line integral admits of further transformation by means of the relations
{{block center|<math>\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial\nu}\cos(x,\nu)-\frac{\partial w}{\partial s'}\cos(y,\nu),</math>}}
{{block center|<math>\int\cos(x,\nu)\cos(y,\nu)\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\frac{\partial w}{\partial s'}ds'=-\int\frac{\partial}{\partial s'}\left\{\cos(x,\nu)\cos(y,\nu)\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\right\}wds'.</math>}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
